title: 5 reasons to not lift heavy weight DEBUNKED
summary: NH debunks five excuses for avoiding heavy weights: it's dangerous, it's ego, it's unnecessary for size, isolation beats barbells, and we're not powerlifters. He argues heavy compounds with good technique are how naturals accumulate tonnage and grow.
claims: With solid technique, lifting at 90% carries little more risk than at 60%; risk rises mainly near a true 1RM
The first two reps at 70-80% should be fast
People who find heavy lifting dangerous treat it as do-or-die and ignore technique
Rules for heavy lifting: slow negatives, identical reps, consistent rep speed, no ugly grinders, good technique from the start, reps in the tank
He lifts heavy every single day because that's how naturals get big
Everything is dangerous if you don't know what you're doing; take calculated risks
Everything we do in the gym feeds our ego, and having an ego is healthy
He trains alone in his gym and still lifts heavy
Handling heavy weight builds confidence, which he believes contributes to higher testosterone
Studies showed expansive postures raise testosterone and GH
Ego-lifting accusations try to shame you out of being great
Even if 30% intensity built equal size, it's impractical time-wise compared with 70%
If your main lifts haven't progressed in two years, your tonnage hasn't and your physique won't have
People who avoid heavy weights plateau and then talk about the natural limit
Natural bodybuilding correlates with tonnage, and compounds give the most tonnage fastest in full ROM
Isolation-only training sends little tonnage to small muscles; machine-only guys stay small unless enhanced
Pros use machines for lower injury risk and grow anyway on drugs; copying them leaves naturals with a fraction of the tonnage
Most pros take Phil Heath's machine road rather than Ronnie Coleman's heavy compounds
The bodybuilding vs powerlifting ego war makes bodybuilders shun compounds; barbells were essential to bodybuilders in the 1940s-50s
Skinny lifters should start with compounds, build them slowly with perfect technique, and add patterns and isolation as they go
Novice programs over-focus on compounds; that's a strength bias
Refusing to squat means small legs for life
